Dysmenorrhea

Several trials and a meta-analysis reported lower menstrual pain, including pooled evidence versus sham. Results differed against active medication, and the 119-person open study had no control group. The best wavelength and schedule remain undetermined.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Several trials and a meta-analysis reported lower menstrual pain, including pooled evidence versus sham. Results differed against active medication, and the 119-person open study had no control group. The best wavelength and schedule remain undetermined.

Summary of the Evidence

The indication category contains 15 database records, representing 15 unique titles. There are eight completed human reports, one protocol, one narrative review, one meta-analysis, four mouse publications, and three in-vitro entries that overlap the mouse research. The meta-analysis reviewed 12 randomized trials across low-level laser, high-intensity laser, and polarized-light treatments; it pooled three low-level-light trials against sham. The review and primary trials overlap and must not be added as new experiments.

Human and clinical evidence

The meta-analysis found lower pain after 12 weeks of low-level light treatment than sham in three trials involving 150 participants. Two earlier double-blind studies used 610-nm red visible light delivered by an adhesive device before menstruation and reported larger pain reductions than sham; the 2016 trial also found lower analgesic use (Shin et al. 2012; Hong et al. 2016; Ang et al. 2025).

A 2025 randomized study tested 810-nm near-infrared laser acupuncture against electroacupuncture in 114 participants and reported improvement with both approaches (Chien et al. 2025). In a separate multicenter comparison, combined oral contraception produced a larger pain-score reduction than light treatment (Zhu et al. 2022). An open 119-person study reported large within-group pain and symptom-score reductions over three cycles, but without a control group those changes cannot establish comparative efficacy (Yi et al. 2026). Other active-comparator studies include high-intensity laser, which is not equivalent to low-level PBM.

Animal evidence

Four unique mouse publications examined induced dysmenorrhea. Red 630-nm light reduced pain behavior and prostaglandin imbalance in one model, with pulsed delivery performing better than continuous-wave exposure. Other experiments reported lower uterine swelling, oxidative stress, and inflammatory measures. A wavelength comparison also found red light had a greater effect on pain behavior than blue visible light at 460 nm, near-infrared light at 850 nm, or thermal treatment (Fu et al. 2025; Fu et al. 2024).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Cell experiments within three mouse-paper records used human uterine smooth-muscle cells. Red-light exposure reduced reactive oxygen species and restored several measured calcium, ATP, and mitochondrial-potential measures in stimulated cells. These findings overlap the animal publications and do not independently show pain relief in patients.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Human protocols include 610-nm red adhesive light for five days before menstruation, 810-nm near-infrared laser acupuncture at 2.5 J/cm² per point, and a 640-nm red LED used for 30 minutes daily during the week before menstruation. Mouse work compared pulsed and continuous red light and tested 460-nm blue, 630-nm red, and 850-nm near-infrared exposures. No head-to-head human dose-finding study identifies an optimal wavelength or schedule.

Interpretation

The pooled sham-controlled result and several individual trials support short-term pain reduction with some light protocols. Active-treatment comparisons are less consistent, and one favored oral contraceptives. Animal and cell experiments provide supporting biological results, but the available studies do not establish one preferred clinical regimen.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for short-term pain reduction versus sham in primary dysmenorrhea Low for superiority over active treatment or a preferred protocol
Publications and records15 database records and 15 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Several controlled trials and a meta-analysis report reduced pain versus sham, but the pooled result combines small studies and protocols, and one active-comparator trial favored oral contraceptives. The findings support a short-term effect for some regimens, not a settled protocol. A larger sham-controlled trial with common pain, function, and medication measures would strengthen the assessment.
